title: The role of visual signals and face patterns in African forest monkeys (guenons) of the genus Cercopithecus
Social complexity parallels vocal complexity: a comparison of three non-human primate species
abstract: Social factors play a key role in the structuring of vocal repertoires at the individual level, notably in non-human primates. Some authors suggested that, at the species level too, social life may have driven the evolution of communicative complexity, but this has rarely been empirically tested. Here, we use a comparative approach to address this issue. We investigated vocal variability, at both the call type and the repertoire levels, in three forest-dwelling species of Cercopithecinae presenting striking differences in their social systems, in terms of social organization as well as social structure. We collected female call recordings from twelve De Brazza's monkeys (Cercopithecus neglectus), six Campbell's monkeys (Cercopithecus campbelli) and seven red-capped mangabeys (Cercocebus torquatus) housed in similar conditions. First, we noted that the level of acoustic variability and individual distinctiveness found in several call types was related to their importance in social functioning. Contact calls, essential to intra-group cohesion, were the most individually distinctive regardless of the species, while threat calls were more structurally variable in mangabeys, the most “despotic” of our three species. Second, we found a parallel between the degree of complexity of the species' social structure and the size, diversity, and usage of its vocal repertoire. Mangabeys (most complex social structure) called twice as often as guenons and displayed the largest and most complex repertoire. De Brazza's monkeys (simplest social structure) displayed the smallest and simplest repertoire. Campbell's monkeys displayed an intermediate pattern. Providing evidence of higher levels of vocal variability in species presenting a more complex social system, our results are in line with the theory of a social-vocal coevolution of communicative abilities, opening new perspectives for comparative research on the evolution of communication systems in different animal taxa.

title: Social familiarity affects Diana monkey (Cercopithecus diana diana) alarm call responses in habitat-specific ways
abstract: Male Diana monkeys produce loud and acoustically distinct alarm calls to leopards and eagles that propagate over long distances, much beyond the immediate group. Calling is often contagious, with neighbouring males responding to each other’s calls, indicating that harem males communicate both to local group members and distant competitors. Here, we tested whether male Diana monkeys responding to each other’s alarm calls discriminated familiar from unfamiliar callers in two populations in Taï Forest (Ivory Coast) and on Tiwai Island (Sierra Leone). At both sites, we found specific acoustic markers in male alarm call responses that discriminated familiar from unfamiliar callers, but response patterns were site-specific. On Tiwai Island, males responded to familiar males’ eagle alarms with ‘standard’ eagle alarm calls, whereas unfamiliar males triggered acoustically atypical eagle alarms. The opposite was found in Taï Forest where males responded to unfamiliar males’ eagle alarm calls with ‘standard’ eagle alarms, and with atypical eagle alarms to familiar males’ calls. Moreover, only Taï, but not Tiwai, males also marked familiarity with the caller in their leopard-induced alarms. We concluded that male Diana monkeys encode not only predator type but also signaller familiarity in their alarm calls, although in population-specific ways. We explain these inter-site differences in vocal behaviour in terms of differences in predation pressure and population density. We discuss the adaptive function and implications of this behaviour for the origins of acoustic flexibility in primate communication.

title: Old world monkey vocalizations: adaptation to the local habitat?
Primate communication. Edited by Charles T. Snowdon, Charles H. Brown, and Michael R. Petersen
Symbols are not uniquely human
abstract: Modern semiotics is a branch of logics that formally defines symbol-based communication. In recent years, the semiotic classification of signs has been invoked to support the notion that symbols are uniquely human. Here we show that alarm-calls such as those used by African vervet monkeys (Cercopithecus aethiops), logically satisfy the semiotic definition of symbol. We also show that the acquisition of vocal symbols in vervet monkeys can be successfully simulated by a computer program based on minimal semiotic and neurobiological constraints. The simulations indicate that learning depends on the tutor-predator ratio, and that apprentice-generated auditory mistakes in vocal symbol interpretation have little effect on the learning rates of apprentices (up to 80% of mistakes are tolerated). In contrast, just 10% of apprentice-generated visual mistakes in predator identification will prevent any vocal symbol to be correctly associated with a predator call in a stable manner. Tutor unreliability was also deleterious to vocal symbol learning: a mere 5% of "lying" tutors were able to completely disrupt symbol learning, invariably leading to the acquisition of incorrect associations by apprentices. Our investigation corroborates the existence of vocal symbols in a non-human species, and indicates that symbolic competence emerges spontaneously from classical associative learning mechanisms when the conditioned stimuli are self-generated, arbitrary and socially efficacious. We propose that more exclusive properties of human language, such as syntax, may derive from the evolution of higher-order domains for neural association, more removed from both the sensory input and the motor output, able to support the gradual complexification of grammatical categories into syntax.

Psychobiological development in primates: Introduction to joint special issue with Developmental Psychobiology
abstract: The disciplines of primatology and developmental psychobiology have long been intertwined, and informed by each other. Pioneering work in primates by developmental psychobiologists like Steven Suomi, Melinda Novak, William Mason, Lynn Fairbanks, Marty Reite, and Gene Sackett has led to substantial insight on the behavioral, emotional, and physiological changes that occur during development in primates (Brumley, 2020). What do we gain by studying development in nonhuman primates, our closest relatives? Submissions to this issue highlight the diversity within the Primate Order. Our authors work with primates of Central and South America (common marmosets; golden lion tamarins; squirrel monkeys; capuchins; and spider monkeys); prosimians (Coquerel's sifaka); apes (orangutans and chimpanzees, humans); and cercopithecines (olive baboons; blue monkeys; and the redoubtable rhesus macaque). While few of the studies compared multiple species within a study, many of the same tools (i.e., Primate Neonatal Neurobehavioral Assessment; social network analysis; etc.) allow us to make some comparative assessments across primate species. In addition to a better understanding of primate development for its own sake, nonhuman primates also aid in our understanding of human behavior, physiology, and health (Phillips et al., 2014). A better comparative understanding of development makes for better nonhuman primate models for health. In this special joint issue of the American Journal of Primatology (AJP) and Developmental Psychobiology (DPB), several themes emerged, both classic and cutting‐edge. The influence of early life social environment on development has been, and still is, a central theme in developmental psychobiology. In the current issue, our understanding is expanded both in breadth by studies of wild or free‐ranging primates, and in depth by pain‐staking laboratory studies. Thompson and Cords, in wild blue monkeys (Cercopithecus mitis stuhlmanni) showed sex‐specific effects of mother's affiliative behavior in predicting the affiliative behavior of their offspring as juveniles. These effects were specific to maternal behavior during early infancy, not maternal behavior throughout development, echoing rodent studies which have found critical windows for impacts of different exposures. Rapaport found that despite the cooperative breeding system of wild golden lion tamarins (Leontopithecus rosalia), older siblings provided fewer food transfers than parents. In DPB, most explored the importance of secondary attachments (to siblings or other animals) for wild infant olive baboons (Papio anubis) with poorly responsive mothers; while Verderane, working with wild capuchins (Sapajust libidinosus) explored face‐to‐face interactions between mothers and infants, and its function to promote communication and care. Cognitive and personality development was also a theme. Arre found that infant and juvenile rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) from a free‐ranging population on Cayo Santiago, show different patterns of performance on a theory of mind test, than do human infants. Murphy and Dettmer (DPB) explored cognitive and emotional development in nursery and mother‐peer‐reared rhesus infants, finding emotional, but no major cognitive differences between the rearing types. They also found predictive effects of these emotional differences at 1 month on cognitive differences at 8–10 months. Mulholland (DPB), also using the Primate Neonatal Neurobehavioral Assessment explored similar questions in nursery‐reared squirrel monkeys, and found multiple developmental differences between nursery‐reared and mother‐reared infants. In AJP, Delval and colleagues documented changes in measures of personality in wild capuchin infants (Sapajus xanthosternos) over development; while Wood and colleagues found that neonatal temperament in rhesus monkeys predicted adolescent alcohol intake. Sociosexual development in adolescent females was an emerging theme, with O'Connell exploring proceptive behavior in the context of developing sexual maturity in wild orangutans (Pongo pygmaeus wurmbii). Rodrigues, in human primates, found that maternal relationship quality was predictive of close female friendships, and fewer depressive symptoms, in adolescent girls. Social network analysis is an exciting tool being used to ask questions about social connections in novel ways. Boeving and colleagues explored juvenile and adult social relationships in spider monkeys (Ateles fusciceps rufiventris), finding different network dynamics for different behaviors and age groups. In rhesus monkeys, Wooddell and colleagues found that high‐ranking monkeys were more central, with mother's rank predicting son's centrality in social play networks. Endocrine and reproductive development was also a major focus in this issue, especially with regard to adolescent development. Carosi and colleagues adapted a technique for measuring clitoral length in hyenas and applied it to female tufted capuchins (Sapajus spp.) in a cross‐sectional study. Sabbi and colleagues documented age‐related changes in cortisol production in wild chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii), similar to developmental changes seen in humans. However, adrenarche started earlier in chimpanzees and there were no sex differences, unlike in humans. Just as early caregiving is central to infant development in primates, understanding of the hormonal cues for caregivers is important. Taylor and colleagues (DPB) manipulated the neuropeptides oxytocin and vasopressin in mothers, fathers, and older siblings in common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus).
